action_criteria.expected_evidence: Language-predominant impairment on MMSE and MoCA (repetition, naming with phonological errors, fluency) with informant-confirmed progressive decline, relatively spared day-to-day memory and behaviour, and preserved independence in instrumental activities
action_criteria.label: Perform a structured cognitive assessment with informant history, a per-domain profile and an explicit account of daily function
action_criteria.rationale: The language-predominant profile and preserved instrumental independence define the syndrome and its stage before any biomarker is interpreted [PPA_2011] [NIA_AA_MCI_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Impaired naming and length-dependent sentence repetition with phonological errors, preserved single-word comprehension, object knowledge, grammar and motor speech, and preserved episodic memory
action_criteria.label: Order comprehensive neuropsychological and language testing to classify the aphasia and set a baseline
action_criteria.rationale: Formal naming, repetition, comprehension and motor speech testing distinguishes the logopenic from the semantic and nonfluent variants of primary progressive aphasia [PPA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No reversible cause: TSH, B12, folate, homocysteine, electrolytes, renal and liver function normal; HbA1c 5.8% above range
action_criteria.label: Order the cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
action_criteria.rationale: Thyroid, B12, folate and metabolic causes must be excluded before a neurodegenerative diagnosis is made, and comorbid vascular risk identified [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Asymmetric left-greater-than-right posterior perisylvian and inferior parietal cortical atrophy with preserved hippocampi; no infarct or mass
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with a dementia protocol to define the pattern of atrophy and exclude a structural or vascular cause of the aphasia
action_criteria.rationale: A progressive aphasia needs MRI to exclude a left hemisphere infarct, mass or other structural lesion and to show the regional atrophy pattern of the PPA variant [NIA_AA_2011] [PPA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amyloid positivity: decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio with raised p-tau181, or a positive amyloid PET
action_criteria.label: Establish amyloid status with CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET when the result would change management
action_criteria.rationale: Either CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau or amyloid PET establishes amyloid status; one conclusive test is enough, and here it decides whether Alzheimer pathology rather than frontotemporal lobar degeneration underlies the aphasia [NIA_AA_2018] [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Asymmetric left posterior temporal and inferior parietal hypometabolism with relative frontal sparing
action_criteria.label: Consider FDG-PET after the core assessment if the variant or the underlying pathology remains uncertain
action_criteria.rationale: Left temporoparietal hypometabolism supports the logopenic variant, whereas anterior temporal or frontal hypometabolism points to frontotemporal lobar degeneration [Foster_2007].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in APP, PSEN1 or PSEN2
action_criteria.label: Offer an early-onset Alzheimer gene panel only after pre-test genetic counselling; do not use APOE genotype as a diagnostic test
action_criteria.rationale: Onset at about 60 makes APP, PSEN1 and PSEN2 testing an option to discuss, but the only affected relative had late-onset dementia, so a pathogenic variant is unlikely and the result would inform family counselling rather than the diagnosis [ACMG_NSGC_2011].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the progressive language deficit to depression or retirement stress; it worsened while his mood responded to sertraline
Do not use APOE genotyping to make or exclude the diagnosis
required_recommendations: Obtain collateral history from an informant who knows the patient well

Disclose the diagnosis of logopenic primary progressive aphasia with its likely Alzheimer cause, explain the expected course, and discuss advance care planning, durable power of attorney and future decisions while he can still take part
Refer to speech and language therapy for assessment and communication strategies [PPA_2011].

Offer amyloid biomarker testing (CSF or amyloid PET) if a biological diagnosis would change management, such as eligibility for anti-amyloid treatment or diagnostic uncertainty; one conclusive test is sufficient [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].
Offer genetic testing only with pre-test and post-test genetic counselling; the result informs the family and not the patient's diagnosis [ACMG_NSGC_2011].
Manage vascular risk: review blood pressure control against target (138/84 mmHg today on lisinopril), continue rosuvastatin, and address HbA1c 5.8% with diet and regular exercise
Continue sertraline and review mood at follow-up; the depression is a comorbidity that improved, while the aphasia progressed
Arrange neurological, language and functional reassessment in 6 to 12 months, and review driving and financial safety as language and function change

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardiac symptom or syncope to justify it in this case
Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication in this presentation
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; no arrhythmia, syncope, or palpitations described
Head CT adds little when MRI is available; MRI is the preferred structural modality for dementia workup
EEG is non-specific in Alzheimer's disease and not part of the routine dementia workup; reserved for suspected seizures, encephalopathy, or rapidly progressive dementia

accepted: Logopenic variant primary progressive aphasia (lvPPA) due to Alzheimer's disease

differential.key_features: Against: single-word comprehension (PPVT 85th percentile) and object knowledge (Pyramids and Palm Trees 96%) are preserved, errors are phonological rather than semantic, and atrophy is posterior perisylvian rather than anterior temporal
Against: speech is fluent and grammatical, motor speech is normal with no apraxia of speech, and the frontal operculum is preserved on MRI

differential.diagnosis: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration (TDP-43 or tau) presenting as PPA
differential.key_features: FTLD can underlie any PPA variant; against it here: the logopenic phenotype, left temporoparietal hypometabolism, and amyloid positivity with raised p-tau181 point to Alzheimer pathology. Incidental amyloid at 62 is possible but does not explain raised p-tau
Gradual progression over two years rather than abrupt onset; MRI shows atrophy and no infarct
Language testing shows true anomia, phonological errors and a repetition deficit, and the aphasia progressed after mood improved on sertraline

key_clinical_evidence: The logopenic variant of primary progressive aphasia is defined by impaired single-word retrieval and sentence repetition with spared single-word comprehension and motor speech; it is most often caused by Alzheimer pathology [PPA_2011].
Preserved hippocampal volumes do not argue against Alzheimer disease in an atypical variant: the atrophy follows the left posterior perisylvian language network

In an atypical presentation, amyloid and tau biomarkers decide between Alzheimer pathology and frontotemporal lobar degeneration; one conclusive test (CSF or amyloid PET) is enough [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET]
A progressive language disorder that worsens while mood improves on treatment should not be attributed to depression

His wife reports progressive word-finding decline over two years with unchanged day-to-day memory and behaviour. metadata.diagnostic_challenge: Differentiating logopenic variant PPA from other PPA variants and recognizing AD as the underlying pathology in an atypical language-predominant presentation initially attributed to depression
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Required core: structured assessment with informant and functional staging, neuropsychological and language testing, the cognitive laboratory panel, and brain MRI. Optional: one amyloid biomarker test (CSF or amyloid PET), FDG-PET for the variant question, and APP/PSEN1/PSEN2 testing after counselling.
metadata.educational_value: Teaches recognition of lvPPA as an atypical AD variant, the importance of differentiating PPA subtypes, and the role of biomarkers in confirming neurodegenerative pathology in atypical presentations
key_educational_points: Logopenic variant PPA is the PPA subtype most commonly caused by underlying Alzheimer disease
Word-finding difficulty with phonological paraphasias and impaired sentence repetition, with preserved comprehension of single words, characterizes lvPPA
Preserved hippocampal volumes do not exclude AD; atypical variants target other cortical regions
Depression can delay diagnosis of neurodegenerative disease when cognitive symptoms are attributed to psychiatric illness
Amyloid biomarkers (CSF or amyloid PET, one conclusive test) establish Alzheimer pathology in atypical presentations
Genetic testing is optional and requires pre-test counselling; APOE is not used to diagnose Alzheimer disease
Staging follows daily function: a patient with PPA who remains independent in instrumental activities is not yet at the dementia stage

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. James Washington is a 62-year-old right-handed retired high school English teacher who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic for evaluation of progressive word-finding difficulty over the past two years. His wife, who accompanies him, first noticed that he began having frequent pauses mid-sentence while teaching, searching for common words that he would previously have used effortlessly. He would often substitute a related but incorrect word or produce phonological errors such as saying 'aminal' for 'animal' or 'hostipal' for 'hospital.' His students and colleagues began to notice these difficulties during his final year of teaching. He retired two years ago, and while he initially attributed his language problems to stress and burnout, the difficulties have continued to worsen. His wife reports that he now frequently loses his train of thought mid-sentence and cannot repeat back sentences longer than about five words. He struggles to follow complex conversations, especially in group settings, and has difficulty understanding sentences with complex syntax, though he can understand individual words and short phrases without trouble. He has particular difficulty with phone conversations where he cannot rely on visual context. Despite these language deficits, his episodic memory remains remarkably intact. He remembers appointments, recent conversations (even if he struggles to articulate his thoughts), recent news events, and daily routines without difficulty. He has not gotten lost, does not repeat questions, and manages his medications independently. His wife notes no personality changes, no behavioral disinhibition, and no significant executive dysfunction beyond the language impairment. He continues to manage their household finances and performs daily activities independently apart from avoiding situations requiring extended conversation. He was evaluated by a psychiatrist 6 months ago who diagnosed depression related to retirement and started sertraline 100 mg daily. His mood has improved significantly, but the language difficulties have continued to worsen despite mood improvement, prompting this referral. He denies headaches, seizures, visual changes, weakness, numbness, or swallowing difficulty.
